newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares, bonds rise on Yeltsin's address.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares, bonds rise on Yeltsin's address.

text.p: Russian shares and MinFin bonds edged up on Thursday as investors were encouraged by the sight of a healthy President Boris Yeltsin addressing parliament, traders and dealers said.
The Russian Trading System index of 23 shares rose by 0.95 percent to 314.07 on $40.62 million in total market volume.
"The fact that Yeltsin pronounced his address in quite a firm voice and even raised his eyes to the hall made a positive impact on the market," a trader with a Western investment company said.
Yeltsin, looking suprisingly fit and active in his broadcast address after a heart operation and pneumonia, slammed the government for slow economic reforms and called for more order in the economy.
He forecast two percent growth of gross domestic product in 1997 and criticised natural monopolies for unjustified prices.
On the share market local operators bought shares, but Western investors refrained from active buying, traders said.
They said prices were still too high for purchases, adding that Western investors -- the major players on the Russian share market -- were no longer ready to buy anything at any prices.
Prices have drifted down in the last few weeks and the index is 10 percent below February 19 record of 347.11.
Utility UES rose to $0.2115 from $0.2085 at Wednesday's close, Surgutneftegaz oil company rose to $0.793 from $0.765, LUKoil fell to $13.70 from $13.80 and utility Mosenergo was $1.340 after $1.348.
The market was waiting for new appointments, including the rumoured appointment of presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais as First Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the economy.

However, by the close of business details of a cabinet reshuffle had not been announced. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said he would reshuffle the government within days, but gave no further details.
Yeltsin's lively speech prevented prices of dollar-denominated MinFin bonds from falling ahead of Friday's U.S. payrolls data, dealers said.
MinFins have fallen in the last few days with other emerging debt since remarks by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan taken as suggesting an early rise in interest rates.
"Prices rose in the morning as Yeltsin's address was lively and active. Then prices eased as somebody decided to take profits," said an IFCI-Moscow Partners Bank dealer.
Treaury bills ignored Yeltsin's speech, with long-dated paper falling about 0.4 percent.

The rouble, strictly controlled by the Central Bank, was not affected by Yeltsin's statement and firmed to about 5,692 to the dollar as banks bought funds to make monthly compulsory reserve payments and to invest in government securities, dealers said.
